core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of community-acquired pneumonia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Evaluate oxygenation and severity promptly, investigate pneumonia and competing cardiac or thromboembolic causes, and consider antibiotics only when clinically indicated after assessment.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive shortness of breath for 3 days

Key HPI features: breathless on exertion (stairs, walking fast), orthopnoea (hard to sleep lying flat), started with a mild cough now productive of yellowish sputum, bilateral chest tightness/pressure worse on deep inspiration, no haemoptysis
Objective/Exam findings: O2 saturation, RR, HR, temperature, chest auscultation, CXR, FBC, CRP; consider BNP/ECG given cardiac concern.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that the absence of a high fever rules out community-acquired pneumonia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Congestive heart failure exacerbation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, or sepsis.
management_principles: Obtain clinician-directed chest imaging and investigations, including ECG and cardiac testing when indicated by orthopnoea or chest pressure.
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Use antibiotic, oxygen, and other treatments only when clinically indicated and clinician-directed.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: progressive shortness of breath for 3 days

breathless on exertion (stairs, walking fast), orthopnoea (hard to sleep lying flat), started with a mild cough now productive of yellowish sputum, bilateral chest tightness/pressure worse on deep inspiration, no haemoptysis
reference_soap.objective: O2 saturation, RR, HR, temperature, chest auscultation, CXR, FBC, CRP; consider BNP/ECG given cardiac concern.
reference_soap.assessment: Likely community-acquired pneumonia / lower respiratory tract infection. DDx: heart failure exacerbation, COPD/asthma exacerbation, PE, occupational lung disease.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange prompt clinician-directed chest imaging, oxygenation assessment, and blood tests; obtain ECG and cardiac testing when indicated by orthopnoea or chest pressure, and assess PE risk. Consider antibiotics only when clinically indicated after severity assessment. Seek emergency care for hypoxemia, respiratory distress, sepsis features, syncope, or chest pressure concerning for ACS or PE.

learning_objectives: Characterise dyspnoea systematically: onset, triggers, orthopnoea, exertional tolerance
Screen for cardiac vs respiratory vs occupational causes
Elicit occupational exposure history relevant to lung disease
Address the patient's ICE — specifically her fear of a cardiac cause

teaching.one_liner: An acute lower respiratory infection causing cough with purulent sputum, pleuritic chest discomfort, and breathlessness; assess severity and alternative cardiopulmonary causes.
red_flags: Use of accessory muscles at rest
Syncope or chest pressure concerning for acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism

must_ask.say: Have you noticed your phlegm becoming thicker, greener, or increasing in amount?
Are you getting short of breath even while resting or propping up on extra pillows at night?
Have you had a fever, chills, sweats, or felt generally unwell?
How many packs of cigarettes did you smoke per day and for how long?
Have you recently been in hospital, had problems swallowing, or been exposed to anyone with a respiratory infection?

history.answer: I've been having trouble catching my breath for the past three days, and it's been getting steadily worse.
It started gradually three days ago as a mild tightness, but it has become progressively harder to breathe each day.
I get winded just walking up one flight of stairs or hurrying on flat ground, though resting helps catch my breath.
The breathlessness is constant rather than sudden attacks. I had a similar feeling five years ago when I was hospitalised with pneumonia.
It's uncomfortable and harder to breathe when I lie flat on my back, so I've been propping myself up with two pillows.
Walking fast and going up stairs make it much worse, while resting helps ease it. Cold air, dust, and animals don't seem to trigger it.
No, I haven't noticed any wheezing, squeaking, or whistling noises when I breathe.
I had a dry cough at first, but now I'm coughing up thick, yellowish phlegm several times a day.
Yes, I've felt hot and feverish with mild shivering since yesterday, though I haven't checked my temperature with a thermometer.
I feel a tight pressure across both sides of my chest, and it hurts more when I take a deep breath.
No, my heart isn't racing or skipping beats, and I haven't felt lightheaded or passed out.
No, there is definitely no blood in my phlegm.
No, I haven't noticed any swelling in my legs or feet, and my weight hasn't gone up.
Neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I haven't had recent surgery, bed rest, long flights, or taken any hormones.
I feel drained and worn out from the sickness, but I haven't looked pale, had heavy periods, or seen black stools.
I haven't had any tingling in my hands or around my mouth, though I am quite worried this might be my heart.
I've never had asthma, emphysema, or heart problems, and I don't use any prescription inhalers.
I only take my usual blood pressure pill; I don't use beta-blockers, aspirin, pain medicines, or any chemotherapy.
I haven't choked on food or had trouble swallowing, and nobody around me at home has been sick.
I thought it was just a bad cold at first, but it hasn't gone away and keeps getting heavier.
I'm terrified this might be something wrong with my heart, or a repeat of the severe pneumonia I had five years ago.
I want to find out what my test results show and get reassurance that my heart is doing fine.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure about two years ago, but I don't have diabetes or any other chronic conditions.
I was admitted to the hospital five years ago for severe pneumonia, but I've never had surgery.
I take amlodipine five milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure, and I don't take any herbal remedies or supplements.
No, I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or latex.
I used to smoke about half a pack a day for ten years, but I completely quit ten years ago.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine during celebrations, maybe two or three times a year.
I worked in a textile factory for nearly fifteen years around fabric dust, and I live at home with my husband.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away in his late seventies, but there's no family history of heart attacks or lung diseases.
My last period started two weeks ago and my cycles are regular; there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 130/82 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and body temperature 38.2°C.
Mild tachypnea without visible accessory muscle use or acute respiratory distress at rest.
Jugular venous pressure is normal with no visible jugular venous distension.
Symmetrical chest expansion with increased tactile fremitus over the right lower lung base and no chest wall tenderness.
Dullness to percussion over the right lower lung base, with resonant percussion over all other lung fields.
Late inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung base, with clear vesicular breath sounds on the left.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, gallops, rubs, or third heart sound.
No pretibial or pedal pitting edema on either lower extremity.
Both calves are symmetrical without swelling, warmth, erythema, or tenderness.
Skin is warm and flushed without cyanosis, pallor, rash, or digital clubbing.
